column5: PAG 2018 intensity in METs (1 MET = energy use sitting at rest): light under 3.0 (slow walking at 2 mph or less, cooking), moderate 3.0 to under 6.0 (brisk walking 2.5 to 4 mph, doubles tennis, raking), vigorous 6.0 or more (jogging, carrying loads upstairs, shovelling snow); four levels: inactive, insufficiently active (some but under 150), active (150 to 300), highly active (over 300 moderate-equivalent a week).

PAG 2018 timing of benefits: a single session of moderate-to-vigorous activity can lower blood pressure, improve insulin sensitivity, improve sleep, reduce anxiety symptoms and improve some aspects of cognition on the same day; disease-risk and physical-function benefits build within days to weeks of consistent activity. Strong evidence that moderate-to-vigorous activity improves sleep quality in adults (falling asleep faster, less waking, more deep sleep).

PAG 2018: health is not the only reason to be active; fun, time with friends and family, the outdoors, feeling energetic and fitness for sport all count, and people should be active for any reasons meaningful to them. Same-day benefits (mood, sleep, anxiety) give a client something to notice before long-term change. Supports the course's autonomy-based motivation lesson.

PAG 2018 sitting: device data show US children and adults sedentary about 7.7 hours a day (55% of waking time); a specific healthy target for sitting time or break frequency could not be set because risk depends on moderate-to-vigorous activity; about 60 to 75 minutes a day of moderate (or 30 to 40 vigorous) appears to remove the excess risk of high sitting; very low sitting reduces but does not remove the risk of doing no moderate-to-vigorous activity.

PAG 2018: the risk of injury to bones, muscles and joints is directly related to the gap between a person's usual level of activity and the new level, so increases should be gradual whatever the starting level; bouts of any length count (the earlier 10-minute minimum was dropped).

PAG 2018 scope: performance-related fitness for athletes and medical screening of competitive athletes are outside the guidelines; programmes may include warm-up, cool-down and stretching whose health benefits are not yet proven but which are common in effective programmes. Useful honesty for the session-design lesson.

PAG 2018: only 26% of US men, 19% of women and 20% of adolescents report enough activity to meet both the aerobic and muscle-strengthening guidelines; about 10% of premature mortality is associated with not meeting the aerobic guideline.

PAG 2018 training principles: overload (more amount or intensity than usual makes the body adapt), progression (small, progressive changes in overload help adaptation while minimising injury risk) and specificity (benefits are specific to the systems doing the work; walking mostly benefits the lower body and cardiovascular system, push-ups mostly the chest, shoulders and upper arms).

PAG 2018: muscle-strengthening has three components, intensity (weight or force relative to what the person can lift), frequency, and sets and repetitions; its effects are limited to the muscles doing the work, so all major groups (legs, hips, back, abdomen, chest, shoulders, arms) need training; bands and body weight count as resistance.

PAG 2018: for aerobic activity, the total amount (for example weekly moderate minutes) matters more for health than any one component of frequency, intensity or duration; definitions separate physical activity (any movement above basal energy use) from exercise (planned, structured, repetitive, aimed at fitness), and name bone-strengthening, balance and flexibility as further types.

PAG 2018 mortality: being active about 150 minutes a week is estimated to give about 33% lower all-cause mortality than inactivity; the steepest gain is from inactive to insufficiently active (about 70% of the benefit by 8.25 MET-hours a week in the pooled curve); there is no lower threshold and no evidence of increased risk even at 3 to 5 times the guideline.

PAG 2018 weight: many people need more than 150 minutes a week to maintain weight, and those losing more than 5% of body weight or keeping a large loss off may need more than 300 minutes; combining calorie restriction with activity works best; muscle-strengthening helps keep lean mass during weight loss; health benefits of activity are largely independent of body weight.

PAG 2018: high-intensity interval training may give similar reductions in cardiovascular risk factors to continuous moderate activity and can improve insulin sensitivity, blood pressure and body composition; adults with overweight or obesity and those at higher cardiometabolic risk tend to gain more from it.

PAG 2018 musculoskeletal: progressive strength work preserves or increases muscle mass, strength and power at all ages, including after stroke, multiple sclerosis, cerebral palsy and spinal cord injury; age-related bone loss is slowed by activity, with important changes beginning around 90 minutes a week; in osteoarthritis, 150 minutes moderate aerobic plus strength improves pain, function and quality of life, and up to 10,000 steps a day does not appear to worsen it; low-intensity walking alone does not seem to reduce fall-related injuries in older adults.

PAG 2018 adverse events: moderate activity such as brisk walking has a low risk of injury or heart attack in generally healthy people; musculoskeletal injury risk rises with total volume (40 miles a week of running carries more risk than 10), contact sports carry more than non-contact, and for the same activity less-fit people are more likely to be injured; cardiac events are rare but risk rises when someone suddenly becomes much more active than usual, greatest when a usually inactive adult does vigorous activity such as shovelling heavy snow; regularly active people have the lowest risk.

PAG 2018 brain health: a single moderate-to-vigorous session reduces state anxiety and improves sleep and some cognition; regular activity reduces trait anxiety (in people with and without anxiety disorders) and depression risk, and improves deep sleep and quality of life; sleep benefits do not depend on time of day, being similar whether activity is more than 8, 3 to 8, or under 3 hours before bed.

PAG 2018 chronic conditions table: osteoarthritis (less pain, better function, no effect on disease progression at recommended levels), hypertension (lower cardiovascular mortality and progression), type 2 diabetes (improved HbA1c, blood pressure, BMI, lipids), breast, colorectal and prostate cancer survivors (lower cancer-specific mortality), multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury and dementia (function and cognition). Pregnancy: moderate activity is safe for generally healthy women and does not raise low birth weight, preterm delivery or early loss.

PAG 2018 key adult guideline: move more and sit less; 150 to 300 minutes moderate or 75 to 150 vigorous or a combination, preferably spread through the week; beyond 300 for additional benefit; muscle-strengthening of moderate or greater intensity for all major muscle groups on 2 or more days. Same core targets as WHO 2020 and the UK CMOs; the US version adds 'preferably spread throughout the week'.

PAG 2018 strength dose: no specific time is recommended, but exercises should be done to the point where another repetition would be difficult; one set of 8 to 12 repetitions per exercise is effective for strength, though 2 or 3 sets may be more effective; gains are progressive and come from more weight or more days; strength is specific to the muscles used, so a variety of exercises is needed for balanced strength. Consistent with the course's proximity-to-failure lesson.

PAG 2018 warm-up, cool-down, flexibility: warm-up and cool-down (slower or lighter versions of the activity) are acceptable and count toward aerobic minutes if at least moderate; a strength warm-up usually means lighter weights; stretching increases range of motion and is an appropriate part of a programme, but its health benefits are unknown, it is unclear whether it reduces injury risk, and stretching time does not count toward the aerobic or strength guidelines.

PAG 2018 starting point for inactive adults: begin at light or moderate intensity in short sessions spread through the week; for example 5 minutes of walking several times a day, 5 to 6 days a week, building to 10 minutes three times a day before raising pace; raise volume gradually over weeks to months; strength can start at 1 day a week at light or moderate effort, then 2 days, raising intensity slightly each week; vary activities to avoid overuse injury.

PAG 2018 aerobic dose: spread over at least 3 days a week, which may also reduce injury and excessive fatigue; 2 minutes moderate counts as 1 minute vigorous, so 150 vigorous is roughly 300 moderate; relative intensity on a 0 to 10 scale puts moderate at 5 or 6 and vigorous from 7 or 8; HIIT has no universally accepted work, rest or ratio definition; less fit or older adults may feel 'moderate' activities as vigorous and should start lighter.

PAG 2018: in general, healthy men and women who plan gradual increases in their weekly activity do not need to consult a health care provider before becoming active; pregnant women and adults with chronic conditions or disabilities are covered separately. Agrees with WHO 2020 and the course's screening stance.

PAG 2018 weight: people gaining weight slowly can add activity toward 300 minutes, cut calories, or both, checking weight regularly to find what works; some need 300 or more minutes plus calorie restriction to reach body-weight goals; all intensities count for energy balance; activity also helps reduce abdominal fat and preserve muscle during weight loss.

PAG 2018 frailty: in frail older adults, multicomponent activity of at least moderate intensity done 3 or more times a week for 30 to 45 minutes per session over at least 3 to 5 months appears most effective for functional ability, and beats a single type of activity; activity improves walking, balance, strength and daily living after hip fracture; older adults returning after an illness such as flu should restart lower and build back gradually; physical inactivity is among the strongest predictors of disability in older people.

PAG 2018 older adults: multicomponent sessions can combine all three types in one session, for example walking, lifting weights, and balance work such as standing on one foot during biceps curls or walking backwards; balance training examples include heel-to-toe walking, sit-to-stand practice and a wobble board; falls programmes generally run about three sessions a week; relative intensity (0 to 10 effort) is a better guide than absolute intensity because older adults use more energy for the same task; rehabilitation strength work counts.

PAG 2018: healthy older adults planning gradual increases generally need not consult a health care professional first; older adults with chronic conditions should talk with theirs about whether conditions limit regular activity and what types and amounts suit them.

PAG 2018 progression rules: injury risk tracks the gap between usual and new activity (the overload); for inactive or low-active people, use relative intensity, start relatively moderate (avoid relatively vigorous efforts such as heavy snow shovelling or running), raise minutes per session and days per week first and intensity later, and watch the relative size of each weekly increase (20 extra minutes is a 10% rise on 200 minutes but 50% on 40); adding 5 to 15 minutes of light-to-moderate walking 2 to 3 times a week carries low injury risk and no known risk of severe cardiac events; older adults may need 2 to 4 weeks to adapt to each new level; less fit people and those with obesity should progress more slowly; after a past overuse injury, progress more slowly next time.

PAG 2018 advice from providers: no evidence shows that consulting a health care provider before activity brings more benefit or fewer adverse events; people without diagnosed chronic conditions and without symptoms such as chest pain or pressure, dizziness or joint pain most likely need not consult; habitually moderate-active people can step up to vigorous gradually without consulting; people who develop new symptoms should consult; seeking advice is most appropriate when contemplating vigorous activity; people with diabetes need attention to blood glucose and footwear.

PAG 2018 injury rates: about one musculoskeletal injury per 1,000 hours of walking for exercise and fewer than four per 1,000 hours of running; fitter people have lower injury risk, more activity raises it; the safest activities are moderate, low impact and non-contact (walking, gardening, cycling, dancing, swimming, golf); walking carries a third or less of the injury risk of running; past injury raises the risk of re-injury to that part; heat, cold, dark and air pollution call for changes of time, place, type or intensity.

PAG 2018 pregnancy: unless there are medical reasons, women can begin or continue light-to-moderate aerobic and strength work, increasing gradually if starting; those habitually vigorous before pregnancy generally need not drastically reduce, provided they stay healthy and discuss adjustments with their provider; perceived exertion (5 to 6 out of 10) or the talk test is a better intensity guide than heart rate in pregnancy; avoid lying on the back after the first trimester (can restrict blood flow to uterus and fetus) and contact, collision, fall-risk or abdominal-trauma activities such as soccer, basketball, horse riding or downhill skiing; postpartum activity does not appear to affect breast-milk volume, composition or infant growth.

PAG 2018 conditions: osteoarthritis, most tolerate 150 minutes moderate (3 to 5 days, 30 to 60 minutes) with low-impact, non-painful activities such as swimming, walking, tai chi and many strength exercises, and activity done safely does not worsen pain or disease; type 2 diabetes, activity can cut risk of death by 30 to 40% and needs attention to blood glucose, footwear and foot injury; hypertension, benefits are greater than in people with normal pressure, with about 90 minutes a week moderate substantially lowering heart-disease risk, and medication may need adjusting as activity rises; cancer survivors should match the plan to abilities and treatment toxicities.

PAG 2018 disability: adults who are able should meet the adult guidelines; when not able, be regularly active according to ability and avoid inactivity; adapt the plan with a health care professional or physical activity specialist (for example arm ergometer or wheelchair work when leg function is affected); some need supervised help with strength work such as lifting weights; the guidelines do not cover therapeutic exercise or rehabilitation.

PAG 2018 case examples show the build-up pattern: a man with multiple sclerosis starts at 20 minutes twice a week on a stationary bike at effort 5 to 6 out of 10 and reaches 160 minutes over months; a woman with knee and hip osteoarthritis meets 160 minutes with home video, chair yoga and mall walks; a pregnant woman swaps a longer walk for swimming when back pain appears. Useful worked examples for the session-design lesson.
